reasoning: Delivering a policy and reviewing a client's program are advisory, often upselling, meetings whose value is in the conversation, which makes them interpersonal. A beneficiary change is a service transaction done with the client present. X captures this cleanly, while Y fragments the visit into four parts and treats advisory conversation as live service.

Quoting a premium and agreeing how it will be paid are steps of one pricing transaction, done either live with the client or afterwards from an application. X splits by where the work is done, as Example D asks. Y further splits calculation from payment setup, which are steps of the same deliverable.

Agents customize personal-lines coverage live while quoting, and build complex multi-risk programs afterwards from collected information. Both are substantial, so the instructions call for X's split by where the work is done, not Y's single back-office proposal.

Selling is persuasion, which the instructions class as interpersonal rather than a service transaction. Completing and submitting the application is a separate written deliverable the underwriter relies on. Y reflects both and notes the overlap with 725 and 726, while X wrongly treats persuasion as live service.

Explaining the pros and cons of policies 'to promote sale' is persuasion in a live conversation. Persuasion is listed under interpersonal, and nothing checkable is produced, so X's interpersonal coding is preferred to Y's live-service coding.

Claim information is exchanged with the client live. The agent then passes a claim notice and documents to the insurer as back-office work after the contact. This is the live-plus-afterwards pattern of Example D, which Y captures and X omits.

Within 'administrative tasks', renewals are mainly processed back-office, and renewal conversations with clients are largely covered by the policy-review statement 718. Y's split into renewal processing and record upkeep fits the statement and avoids double-counting live review time with 718.

The statement includes deciding whether the property is a good risk, and the resulting assessment is passed to the underwriter. The instructions say to split activity that is partly physical and partly desk work, which X does. Y drops the assessment.

Planning the integration produces a plan, while overseeing it is ongoing coordination of the client's staff. X's single unit is a whole project rather than a handed-over item, which the instructions warn against. Y separates the two activities.

Explaining what bookkeeping a client must set up is teaching the client's staff, which the instructions class as interpersonal. It is not a service transaction completed while the customer waits, so Y is preferred.
